section_summary: This section covers U.S. State Department and diplomatic intelligence records from July 1941 to February 1944 concerning political developments and ministerial reorganizations in the Japanese government. Key subjects include the fall of the third Konoe Cabinet and the formation of the military-dominated Tojo Cabinet in October 1941, the resignation of Foreign Minister Shigenori Togo over the creation of the Ministry of Greater East Asia in late 1942, and successive wartime reallocations of economic, munitions, and foreign affairs portfolios under Hideki Tojo through early 1944. A comprehensive 21-page OSS intelligence monograph details the jurisdiction, central administration, and field organization of the Ministry of Greater East Asia across occupied territories, alongside diplomatic reporting from Tokyo, Bern, Moscow, Chungking, and London assessing Japan's continental strategy, Axis relations, and Soviet policy.

subfiles.about: Exhaustive intelligence monograph detailing the statutory authority, central ministry bureaus, advisory councils, and overseas field structure of the Ministry of Greater East Asia.
subfiles.from: Office of Strategic Services (OSS)
subfiles.summary: This comprehensive 21-page OSS intelligence monograph provides an exhaustive organizational analysis of Japan's Ministry of Greater East Asia (Daitōashō), established in late 1942. The report defines the ministry's territorial jurisdiction encompassing all occupied and sphere areas outside Japan proper, Korea, Formosa, and Karafuto, and details its absorption of the China Affairs Board (Kōain), the Manchurian Affairs Board, the Overseas Ministry, and the Foreign Office East Asia Bureau. It profiles Minister Kazuo Aoki, Vice Minister Kumaichi Yamamoto, six specialized technical Councillors, and the four main administrative bureaus (General Affairs, Manchukuo, China, and South Seas). The study further maps the diplomatic and administrative field structure in occupied China and Inner Mongolia under Ambassador Mamoru Shigemitsu and four Ministers Plenipotentiary (at Nanking, Kalgan, Peking, and Shanghai), as well as embassy and consular representations in Manchukuo, French Indo-China, and Thailand, while noting that areas under military administration (Philippines, Malaya, Netherlands East Indies, Burma) remain outside its immediate control.
subfiles.title: OSS Research and Analysis Report: Jurisdiction, Organization and Personnel of Japanese Greater East Asia Ministry

subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.summary: Department cable to Kuibyshev assessing April 1943 cabinet changes: stronger war administration, a Shigemitsu soft policy in China, and continued efforts to preserve Soviet neutrality and mediate a German-Soviet peace.
subfiles.title: State Department Cable No. 221 to Kuibyshev: Analysis of Japanese Cabinet Changes

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting Berlin press coverage and official German assessments of the February 1944 Japanese cabinet changes.
subfiles.from: Leland Harrison, U.S. Minister to Switzerland
subfiles.summary: Harrison reports German papers call Japan's February 1944 cabinet changes a technical reorganization for total war, strengthening Tojo, with Ishiwata and Uchida continuing existing economic policies.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1168 from Bern: German Press Commentary on Japanese Cabinet Reshuffle
